amendments.rule: A target head is the cross-language lexical display anchor: the English token that most directly realizes the source head's lexeme, with English syntax used only to break a genuine tie. Choose the lexical predicate over subjects and auxiliaries (`was gathered` heads on `gathered`), the noun in `of + noun`, and the substantive over a generic English noun supplied to expand it (`living creature` for a substantival adjective heads on `living`; rule 31 gives the test and governs the whole family). Where one morpheme is rendered by a multi-word English preposition, the head is the token carrying the lexeme rather than the connective: `מִן` → *out of* heads on *out*. **Where the ASV recasts one morpheme's relation as a fixed English phrase in which no word realizes that morpheme's own lexeme, head on the content word the phrase turns on, found by rule 31's subtraction test, and never on one of its connectives**: `מִן` → *of one piece with* heads on *piece*, because dropping *piece* leaves the phrase saying nothing while *of*, *one* and *with* are what English spends on the relation, exactly as `מִן` → *by reason of* heads on *reason*. This reaches only a rendering that drops the lexeme; where a word does realize it, the preceding sentence governs and the head stays there. **But a degree word the ASV writes beside a comparative preposition is not the token carrying the lexeme, and the *out of* sentence does not reach it.** Where a comparative `מִן` is rendered by a degree adverb together with the relational word — *more than*, *rather than* — the comparison's own relation is what the morpheme says, and the degree adverb is what English spends on a comparison it writes without one elsewhere, so the unit heads on *than*, exactly as a bare `מִן` → *than* does. Test by the subtraction rules 16, 31 and 43 use: drop *than* and the comparison has no relation left to state, while dropping *more* or *rather* leaves the comparative the ASV writes in that shape throughout. Read which of the two English words the ASV has added rather than which of them stands first, since in *out of* it is the opening word that carries the ablative lexeme and the closing one that is the bare connective, and in *more than* it is the other way about. The corpus aligns `מִן` to *more than* headed on *than* in twenty-five units and to a bare *than* in a hundred and nineteen. **But read that sentence as a ruling about a degree adverb, and not as a direction to head on whichever English word states the relation.** Where a preposition is rendered by a fixed English phrase built on a relational content word and closed by a colourless *to* or *of* — *according to*, *by reason of*, *out of* — that content word is the token carrying the lexeme and the head goes there, never on the connective, whatever relation the source preposition would state if it stood alone. `לְ` → *according to* and `כְּ` → *according to* both head on *according*, because the same subtraction finds that dropping *according* leaves a bare dative or comparative stating some other relation altogether, while dropping *to* leaves the conformity the ASV wrote the phrase for. What the *more than* sentence excludes is a degree adverb English adds to a comparison it writes elsewhere without one; a word the ASV never omits from the phrase is not such an addition, so ask whether the ASV writes the relation without that word before treating it as added. The corpus heads `לְ` → *according to* on *according* in a hundred and seventeen units and on *to* in none. Review this choice independently of the unit's edges.
amendments.why: 1CH.24.3, 1CH.24.4 and 1CH.24.19 each headed a preposition rendered *according to* on *to*, citing rule 24's 'relational word'. That is the *more than* sentence read as a general preference for whichever English word states the relation, which rule 24's own *out of* and *by reason of* sentences contradict and which 117 corpus units contradict outright — the corpus heads לְ → *according to* on *according* and on *to* nowhere. The amendment closes the reading that misled three units in one chapter by naming the case and giving the subtraction that decides it, and it leaves the *more than* ruling and every other clause of the rule standing as they were.

conventions: Where the ASV recasts a Hebrew prepositional predicate or appositional phrase so that the preposition carries its own written English and the copula is left standing beside a predicate the ASV has supplied, this chapter marked the copula `added` together with that supplied predicate rather than giving it to the spent preposition under rule 49. 1CH.24.1 `וְלִבְנֵי אַהֲרֹן מַחְלְקוֹתָם` → *And the courses of the sons of Aaron* ***were these*** puts *were these* in one `added` unit, the `לְ` keeping the *of* the ASV wrote for it; 1CH.24.6 `מִן־הַלֵּוִי` → *the scribe,* ***who was*** *of the Levites* does the same with *who was*, the `מִן` keeping its *of*. Both notes name rule 49's competing reading, which would give the copula to the preposition as `בְכַפֵּיהֶם` → *is in their hands* does. What tipped both units the other way is that the recast English leaves the preposition inside a subject or a modifier rather than heading the clause's predicate, which is the case rule 49's own closing paragraph excludes.

report: Cross-verse check found no construction analysed two ways. The candidate groups that looked like splits are all licensed by the source or by what the ASV wrote: לִפְנֵי fuses to *before* in v2 and splits into *in* / *the presence* in v6 and v31, because rule 30's one-rendering condition is met in the first and unmet in the others; לְ is rendered *to*, *for*, *of* and *Of* in different phrases; v7, v12-v15 and v16 run three different determiner counts rather than three treatments of one construction; v2 and v28 divide their possessive הָיָה clauses identically; בְנוֹ fuses to *Beno* in both v26 and v27; supplied English over a gapped nominal is `added` in both v6 (*one*) and v31 (*those of*).

One real error, and it is a head rather than an edge. 1CH.24.3 (s015), 1CH.24.4 (s029) and 1CH.24.19 (s012) render a preposition by *according to* and head the unit on *to*. Rule 24 heads a multi-word English preposition on the token carrying the lexeme rather than on the connective, and the corpus heads לְ to *according to* on *according* in 117 units and on *to* in none. All three are patched; no source or target edge moves, only target_head.

The verse notes cite rule 24's 'relational word', which is that rule's *more than* carve-out read too widely: *more* is a degree adverb English adds, while *according* is the whole of what distinguishes the phrase from a bare dative. Amendment to rule 24 returned below.

BSB: none of the twelve disagreements is a genuine error. Ten are the documented convention difference (a לְ or a suffix left with no English by a recast possessive clause at v1, v2, v4 and v28; an article the ASV writes no *the* for at v4, v5, v7 and v31; an unrendered waw at v31). The v6 אָחֻז is the third of three occurrences for which the ASV writes two *taken*s, and rule 22 marks one unrepresented; its own marginal note corroborates the doubling.

Left standing deliberately: v1's *were these* and v6's *who was* are the chapter's two debatable calls, each one a supplied copula standing beside a supplied predicate while the preposition holds the *of* the ASV wrote for it. They agree with each other and both notes name rule 49's competing reading, so there is no split to fix; logged as a convention instead of relitigating a single-verse judgment.

The eight added units (v1, v4, v6 twice, v19, v23 twice, v31) were each checked against rule 2's contiguity-and-office test. v23's two italic runs are correctly two units, separated by the ASV's own rendered *Jeriah*.
